passage: Sit, Vaibhav. You want to know why I always carry two tickets? Let me tell you what Yash did at twenty. December, a banking exam in Lucknow, and every newspaper full of fog. I booked the night train, but I also went to the bus stand and bought a seat for later that night, and wrote both timings inside my ticket folder: train at nine, bus at eleven if the train failed. My friends laughed. The train was five hours late. Half the platform sat on their bags staring at the empty tracks. I opened my folder, walked to the bus stand and caught the last bus. I reached the city at dawn with time to wash my face. Two tickets cost me a little. Missing that exam would have cost me a year.

passage:
Bidisha's entrance exam was at ten on Sunday in Lucknow, and she had a seat on the night train from Kolkata. It was December. Her roommate Sabina had been stuck on the same line for six hours last winter because of fog.
"What if the train is late?" Sabina asked.
Bidisha didn't brush it off. She opened the bus booking site and found an overnight bus from Varanasi, where the train stopped at two in the morning. If the train was running more than three hours late at Varanasi, she'd get off and take the 3.30 bus, which reached Lucknow at eight. She booked the bus seat, refundable, and wrote the timings on a card in her wallet.
At Varanasi, the train was running four hours late in thick fog. Bidisha got off, walked to the bus stand with her bag and took the 3.30 bus.
She reached the exam centre at nine.

qa.q: What time did the bus reach Lucknow?
qa.a: The 3.30 bus reached Lucknow at eight.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt when she saw the train running four hours late?
qa.a: She was probably anxious but steady, since she already had a plan and knew exactly where to go.

qa.q: Why was deciding the three-hour rule in advance helpful?
qa.a: Because at two in the morning in fog she didn't have to think or panic; she just followed the rule she had set.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel hearing that Bidisha reached the centre at nine?
qa.a: Sabina may feel relieved and glad that her warning about the fog helped.

Parul's university exam was in Chandigarh at eleven on Monday, and her train from Delhi left at six. In January, fog was always a gamble.
Her friend Chandrika had missed a paper last year when her train crawled in four hours late. So on Friday evening, in their Karol Bagh PG, Parul sat with her phone and worked it out.
Plan A: the 6.00 train, arriving 9.30. Plan B: the 5.30 bus from Kashmere Gate, arriving 10.00. She booked the bus seat too, knowing she could cancel it. Then she wrote on a sticky note: Check train status at 4.30. If delayed over 1 hour, take the bus.
At 4.30 on Monday, the app showed the train delayed by two hours. Parul grabbed her bag and got an auto to Kashmere Gate.
She reached the exam centre at 10.15, forty-five minutes early.

How might Parul have felt when she saw the two-hour delay?
qa.a: She probably felt a rush of worry, but also relieved and ready, since the bus plan was already booked.

qa.q: What else could Parul do to make the plan even safer?
qa.a: She could keep a little cash and the bus ticket printed, in case her phone battery dies during the rush.

qa.q: How might Chandrika see Parul's backup plan?
qa.a: Chandrika may feel glad that her bad experience last year helped Parul avoid the same thing.
